## Why RAG exists {.section-slide}

## The problem RAG solves {.content-slide}

LLMs are trained on the public web. They have not seen:

- Your company's internal SOPs
- Your vendor contracts and SLAs
- Last quarter's post-incident review
- Your specific support runbooks
- The policy your CEO sent on Tuesday

An LLM asked about any of these makes up something plausible — or refuses.

::: notes
The model has a knowledge cutoff and a "no internal documents" handicap.
Both can be addressed by giving the model the right text at the right
moment. That's what RAG is.
:::

## The simplest possible fix {.content-slide}

Before calling the LLM, **paste the relevant document into the prompt**.

That is RAG. Everything else is engineering:

- Which document?
- Which part of it?
- How do you find it fast?
- What do you do when nothing in your library is relevant?

::: notes
This framing matters. RAG is not a magical technique — it's a
discipline for getting the right text into the prompt. The hard work
is selection, not generation.
:::

## The RAG pipeline {.content-slide}

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  Q["User<br/>question"] --> E1["Embed<br/>query"]
  E1 --> R[Retrieve<br/>top-k chunks]
  KB[(Knowledge</br>base)] -.indexed</br>offline.-> R
  R --> P[Chunks</br>+ question]
  P --> LLM[LLM]
  LLM --> A[Answer<br/>+ citations]
```

Two halves: **offline** (build the index) and **online** (answer queries).

::: notes
Students often confuse these. Indexing is a batch job that happens
when documents change. Retrieval is the millisecond-scale per-query
step. We're going to ignore the prompt-building / LLM step in this
deck and focus on how chunks are found in the first place.
:::

## Embeddings and cosine similarity {.section-slide}

## What is an embedding? {.content-slide}

An **embedding model** turns a piece of text into a fixed-length list
of numbers (a vector).

For our model (`api-tgpt-embeddings`): Every text becomes a list of
**1024 floating-point numbers**, regardless of the input length.

```text
"how do I reset my password"
  → [ 0.014, -0.082, 0.337, ..., -0.041 ]   # 1024 numbers
```

The key property: **texts with similar meaning produce vectors that
point in similar directions.**

::: notes
This is not a hash. Two paraphrases of the same idea produce different
exact numbers but very similar directions. That direction-similarity
is what we exploit.
:::

## Cosine similarity, in pictures {.content-slide .smaller}

Imagine each text as an arrow from the origin in some high-dimensional space.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[reset</br>password] -.- B[forgot login]
  A -.- C[invoice wrong]
```

- *reset password* and *forgot login* point in nearly the same direction → high cosine
- *reset password* and *invoice wrong* point in different directions → low cosine

Cosine ranges from -1 to +1. We rank retrieved chunks by their cosine
similarity to the user's query.

::: notes
The geometric intuition is more important than the formula. Cosine
ignores the length of the vector and only cares about the angle.
Don't get hung up on "what does dimension 47 mean?" — these dimensions
are not interpretable individually.
:::

## The math, briefly {.content-slide}

For two vectors $u$ and $v$:

$$\cos(u, v) = \frac{u \cdot v}{\|u\| \cdot \|v\|}$$

If we **pre-normalise** every vector to length 1 (the standard trick),
then $\|u\| = \|v\| = 1$ and cosine reduces to just the dot product
$u \cdot v$.

In numpy: A single matrix-vector multiply $M$, $q$ gives the cosine
similarity of $q$ against every row of $M$ at once.

::: notes
This is why no vector database is needed for small corpora. The
"vector store" is a numpy array; the "search" is one matmul. Fast,
inspectable, no infrastructure.
:::

## Naive RAG {.section-slide}

## Naive RAG in three steps {.content-slide}

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  D[Document] --> C[Chunk it<br/>sliding</br>window]
  C --> E[Embed each</br>chunk]
  E --> M[(Matrix:<br/>rows × 1024)]
  Q[Query] --> EQ[Embed query]
  M --> S{cosine<br/>similarity}
  EQ --> S
  S --> T[Top-k chunks]
```

::: notes
This is the textbook baseline. Chunk by token count, embed verbatim,
cosine retrieval. It works. It also has predictable failure modes,
which is why we go further.
:::

## What naive chunking looks like {.content-slide}

A 300-word document, 100-word chunks with 25-word overlap:

```text
chunk 0:  words   0..100   →  embedding row 0
chunk 1:  words  75..175   →  embedding row 1
chunk 2:  words 150..250   →  embedding row 2
chunk 3:  words 225..325   →  embedding row 3
```

Question: Why the overlap?

::: fragment
Notice in `rag/naive_index.json`:

- Chunks are labelled `window 0`, `window 1`, ...
- The natural `## Identity verification` heading is **destroyed**
- A chunk can split mid-sentence
:::

::: notes
Open `rag/index/naive_index.json` after the eval and let students
read a chunk. The reading experience is jarring — that's the point.
The retrieval system has no idea what each chunk is "about" except
through its embedding.
:::

## Naive RAG: when it works {.content-slide}

For our 18-doc corpus on the eval suite:

- Hit-rate@3 = **8/10** for naive RAG
- Most "obvious" queries hit the right doc

Example: "wrong customer on my invoice" → returns KB-013 (the
billing-export RCA) at position 1 with score 0.529.

When the query keywords overlap the chunk text, naive does fine.

::: notes
Naive is not bad. For many corpora it is the right amount of work.
We use it as the baseline because (a) it really does work, and
(b) the contrast with HyQ is the lesson.
:::

## HyQ — Hypothetical Queries {.section-slide}

## The HyQ idea {.content-slide}

Instead of embedding the chunk text, embed **questions the chunk
answers**.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  D[Document] --> C[Chunk on</br>natural headings]
  C --> G[Ask LLM:<br/>5 questions]
  G --> EQ[Embed questions]
  EQ --> M[(Matrix:<br/>rows × 1024)]
  Q[User query] --> EQuery[Embed query]
  M --> S{cosine}
  EQuery --> S
  S --> R[Top question</br>Parent chunk]
```

::: notes
Two changes from naive:
1. Chunk on ## headings, not by token count
2. Embed LLM-generated questions per chunk, not the chunk text itself
:::

## Why this tends to win on our docs {.content-slide}

1. Our docs were **written as a sequence of self-contained sections.** HyQ respects those boundaries instead of slicing through them.
2. User queries **are questions.** Embeddings of questions live closer to other questions in vector space than to declarative section bodies.
3. The retrieved chunk carries its **real heading** and the **matched question** — so downstream prompts and citations are self-explanatory.

::: notes
The third point is more important than it sounds. A retrieved chunk
with a real heading like "Identity verification" gives the next LLM
call (and any human reviewer) a sense of context that a chunk labelled
`window 1` never can.
:::

## HyQ index shape {.content-slide .smaller}

```python
index = {
  "mode": "hyq",
  "embed_model": "api-tgpt-embeddings",
  "chunks": [
    {
      "chunk_id": "KB-001#1",
      "doc_id": "KB-001",
      "doc_title": "Tier-1 Password Reset SOP",
      "section_heading": "Identity verification (required before any reset)",
      "text": "...",
      "hyq": [
        "How do I verify identity before a reset?",
        "Can I use email verification for password resets?",
        "What if the manager is on PTO?",
        "..."
      ],
      "embedding_rows": [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]   # rows in the embedding matrix
    },
    ...
  ],
  "embeddings": <np.ndarray shape=(505, 1024)>
}
```

- 18 docs → 101 sections → 505 questions → 505 × 1024 = ~2 MB matrix
- No vector database. One JSON file + one `.npy` file.

::: notes
Show this side-by-side with the naive index in class — it makes the
"chunks are destinations, questions are the address book" framing
concrete.
:::

## The eval results {.content-slide .smaller}

Ten hand-picked queries paraphrasing real support situations:

```text
Hit-rate@3: NAIVE = 8/10 (80%)   HyQ = 9/10 (90%)
```

Sample where HyQ wins cleanly:

> *Query:* "how long does the vendor say we have to notify a customer of a breach"
> *Expected:* KB-006 (AuriLite IDP contract — breach notification SLA)
>
> - Naive top-3: KB-003, KB-005, KB-005  ✗ (returns data classification + after-hours)
> - HyQ top-3:   **KB-006**, KB-013, KB-013  ✓

Naive missed because no chunk contains the literal phrase "breach
notification" — HyQ found a hypothetical question that did.

::: notes
This is the kind of win HyQ gets. The doc contains the answer; naive
chunking doesn't surface it because the embedding of the raw chunk
doesn't echo the user's vocabulary. HyQ does, via the generated
question.
:::

## A challenging query {.content-slide .smaller}

> "is there a system change scheduled that could explain the current portal slowness"

Expected: **KB-015 (Q2 2026 change calendar)** — it lists a Customer
Portal upgrade window on 2026-06-07.

Actual:

| Rank | Naive | HyQ |
|-----:|-------|-----|
| 1 | KB-009 portal runbook | KB-010 dashboard runbook |
| 2 | KB-009 portal runbook | KB-009 portal runbook |
| 3 | KB-010 dashboard runbook | KB-009 portal runbook |
| 4 | **KB-015** ← 4th | (not in top 5) |

Naive at least surfaces KB-015 at position 4. HyQ doesn't.

::: notes
Discussion prompt: Why is HyQ *worse* than naive on this one? Walk
students through their hypotheses before showing the next slide. Many
will guess "the calendar doc was written from the wrong perspective."
That's the natural answer — and it's wrong.
:::

## Why it fails — the actual mechanism {.content-slide .smaller}

The user query has two clauses:

- **Cause**: "system change scheduled"
- **Symptom**: "portal slowness"

Dense embeddings weight the **symptom** clause more heavily because
words like *slow*, *down*, *portal* are common, specific, and have
strong neighbours in training data. The query vector ends up pointing
toward "things about slow portals."

The runbooks (KB-009, KB-010) have generated questions like:

- "Why is the dashboard slow at a specific time every night?" → 0.781
- "Why is the portal down every Sunday?" → 0.725

KB-015's best symptom-shaped question only manages 0.661.

::: notes
This is a structural property of dense retrieval, not a flaw of HyQ.
Two-clause queries with unequal vividness get pulled toward the more
vivid clause. The fix is structural too — different retrieval, or
different questions.
:::

## Three ways to fix it {.content-slide}

::: incremental

1. **Hybrid search**: combine cosine with a keyword score (BM25). The literal word *scheduled* appears in KB-015 and almost nowhere else.
2. **Query rewriting**: ask the LLM to split a multi-clause query into single-clause queries, retrieve each, merge results.
3. **Add a question to KB-015** that echoes the user's exact vocabulary. This is HyQ's signature operational fix and the next section is dedicated to it.

:::

::: notes
All three are real techniques. We'll dwell on (3) because it's a
beautiful property unique to HyQ and a great teaching point about the
gap between "good algorithm" and "good operational pattern."
:::

## Patching retrieval by adding questions {.section-slide}

## Adding questions is cheap and additive {.content-slide}

Each new question:

- One embedding API call (~80 tokens, sub-cent at TritonAI rates)
- One row appended to the embedding matrix (~4 KB)
- A one-line append to that chunk's `hyq` list in the JSON

You can do this without re-embedding anything else and without
touching the source documents.

::: notes
This is the operational killer feature of HyQ. The corpus is durable,
chunking is fiddly, but the question list is an additive surface that
you can curate over time.
:::

## Vocabulary matching beats paraphrasing {.content-slide .smaller}

Four candidate questions for the portal-slowness miss, scored against the
user's query:

| Candidate question         | Score | Note |
| -------------------------- | ----- | ---- |
| "Before troubleshooting a **slow** or **down portal**, what **scheduled changes** should I check?" | **0.882** | echoes both clauses |
| "Could **portal slowness** or **downtime** right now be caused by a **scheduled change**?" | **0.874** | echoes both clauses |
| "Why is the **Customer Portal slow** today — is there a **scheduled maintenance** window?" | **0.858** | echoes both clauses |
| "Is there a **planned outage** that explains current **degraded performance**?" | 0.781 | paraphrases — and loses |

Same meaning, different words → 0.10 lower cosine. **You are writing
magnets for embedding similarity, not prose.**

::: notes
This is one of the most important slides in the deck. The lesson
generalises: when patching HyQ for a missed query, echo the customer's
exact words, do not paraphrase. The fourth candidate is the negative
example — semantically equivalent, lexically different, and it loses.
:::

## One question can live on multiple chunks {.content-slide}

The portal-slowness query benefits from **two** docs:

- KB-015 (calendar): *is anything scheduled?*
- KB-009 (runbook): *if not, what's the diagnostic procedure?*

If we add the same patch question to **both** chunks, the de-dup
behaviour in HyQ retrieval surfaces both. Each chunk shows up once,
matched on the same question, with the same score.

> **Chunks are destinations; questions are the address book.**
> One destination can have many addresses. One address can route to
> multiple destinations.

::: notes
Demonstrate this in the live demo. The same patch question pinned to
KB-015 and KB-009 returns both. That is the correct result for this
query — not a workaround.
:::

## The really important point {.section-slide}

## Real customer Q&A beats LLM-generated questions {.content-slide .smaller}

When we built the HyQ index, we asked an LLM:

> "Generate 5 hypothetical questions this section answers."

That gave us questions like "How do I verify identity before a reset?"
— polite, complete, slightly textbook.

**Real customers do not type like that.** Real customers type:

- "i forgot my password help"
- "cant log in pls"
- "portal stuck after sso"
- "tax wrong on my latest invoice"

::: notes
The polite LLM-generated questions point in the rough direction of
what customers ask, but they're systematically displaced. The
embedding model has seen the customer's actual phrasing far more often
than the LLM's clean paraphrase of it.
:::

## What would be better seed data? {.content-slide}

A historical record of **questions customers actually asked** paired
with **the doc that resolved them**.

That's just a ticket log with resolution attribution:

```text
TKT-00042  "cant log in to portal pls help"  →  resolved by KB-001
TKT-00099  "invoice tax wrong after move"    →  resolved by KB-013
TKT-00115  "portal slow today???"            →  resolved by KB-015
...
```

Embed those questions — that's your HyQ index. **Real vocabulary,
real query distribution.**

::: notes
The classroom takeaway: RAG isn't only about clever algorithms. The
operational signal you have access to — past tickets, FAQs, recorded
support conversations — is often the most leveraged input to retrieval
quality. And this repo's workflow already produces exactly that trail
in `data/working/`.
:::

## What does this require operationally? {.content-slide}

The historical data needs **resolution attribution** — each ticket
tagged with which doc resolved it.

- If your support process already writes that down → free training data
- If it doesn't → start now; you'll thank yourself in six months

The ticket workflow in this repo produces that trail
(`data/working/ticket_action_log.csv`) as a side effect of running.
Same pattern: the workflow's audit trail becomes future retrieval's
training data.

::: notes
This connects RAG back to the workflow lesson from the previous deck.
The "AI-assisted process" produces auditable signals that compound:
better workflow → better data → better retrieval → better workflow.
:::

## Wrap-up {.section-slide}

## What we covered {.content-slide .smaller}

| Concept | One-line summary |
| ------- | ---------------- |
| Embedding | text → 1024 floats; meaning maps to direction |
| Cosine similarity | how aligned two vectors are; we use it to rank |
| Naive RAG | chunk by tokens, embed chunks, retrieve by cosine |
| HyQ | chunk by ## heading, embed LLM-generated questions per chunk |
| Two-clause query failure | embedding pulls toward the more vivid clause |
| Patch by adding questions | cheap, additive, vocabulary-driven |
| Real customer Q&A | the best HyQ source data is your own ticket history |

::: notes
Use this as a recap before the live demo. Then run the demo. Then
take Q&A.
:::

## What to play with {.content-slide}

```bash
# Build both indices (uses your TRITONAI_API_KEY)
uv run python -m rag.build_index --mode naive
uv run python -m rag.build_index --mode hyq

# Run the side-by-side eval
uv run python rag/eval.py

# Open the interactive demo
uv run python scripts/rag_demo.py --port 8766
# → http://127.0.0.1:8766
```

Try a query like "portal slowness scheduled change" in the demo and
watch which docs each mode surfaces. Then add a custom question to
KB-015 and see the ranking change.

::: notes
The demo is the lab. The slides are the framing. Encourage students
to "break" the demo — try queries that ought to fail and see which
mode degrades gracefully.
:::
